title: How To Stop Students From Breaking The Same Rule Again And Again me-rule-again-and-again/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using a hypothetical student named Brittany who repeatedly breaks the same rule despite consequences, Michael Linsin distinguishes between inconsistent enforcement (the most common cause of repeated misbehavior) and genuine impulsiveness that overwhelms a student's self-control in the moment. For the latter case, Linsin critiques the common practice of privately reminding an individual student, arguing it singles them out, subtly labels them as incapable of self-control, and reinforces a limiting self-belief. His recommended alternative is to deliver reminders to the entire class rather than to the individual student at the moments known to trigger their misbehavior, so accountability is preserved without stigmatizing the impulsive student. He clarifies this doesn't mean whole-class reminders before every transition—only during the specific moments that tend to trigger recurring misbehavior.
points: Inconsistent enforcement of consequences is identified as the number one reason students repeatedly break the same rule.
For genuinely impulsive students, individual private reminders can inadvertently label them as incapable of self-control, reinforcing a limiting self-belief.
The recommended alternative is to give reminders to the whole class at moments known to trigger the specific student's misbehavior, rather than singling them out.
This approach preserves accountability while avoiding the stigmatizing effect of individualized reminders delivered in front of peers.
Whole-class reminders are only needed at trigger moments, not before every transition or routine.
quotes: Inconsistency is the number one reason students continue to break the same rules again and again.
Questioning, lecturing, forcing assurances, and the like is too personal. It will only alienate her, create friction between you, and ultimately lead to more problems and misbehavior.
You’re telling her in a very subtle way that she is unlike other students, that she alone needs a reminder in order to control herself.
Although it may work in the moment, which is why the strategy is so common, your reminder is actually creating, reinforcing, and cementing a limiting belief she has about herself.
Although Brittany may be the only one who pushes other students while jostling to get in line, you remind everyone.
In time, whole-class reminders combined with faithful accountability will break Brittany of her impulsive rule-breaking.
